title: She outsold Jane Austen but was erased from economic history for pedagogical novels
dek: Her novels far outpaced The Wealth of Nations in readability, yet both readers and economic historians abandoned them once Jane Austen's naturalistic narrative style rose to dominance and didactic fiction fell from favor.
why: If you're curious how economics shifted from storytelling to mathematical modeling, or want a historical lens for understanding economic upheaval in the AI era, this episode offers a rare 19th-century angle.
who: Listeners interested in economic thought history, forgotten female economists, and how fiction spreads ideas—and anyone seeking historical analogies to understand the AI era.
skip: Skip the discussion of her children's book The Cherry Orchard—the hosts themselves admit the story is boring.

points.h: She once outsold Jane Austen during her own lifetime
points.body: A decade ago, journalist Gina Smialek was reporting from the Federal Reserve when she read Robert Heilbroner's The Worldly Philosophers. She found a footnote: David Ricardo had a close friend named Maria Edgeworth, ‘possibly the first woman to think systematically about economic questions.’ This sentence appeared only in later editions and was easily missed. When Gina researched further, she discovered this nearly forgotten writer had once outsold Jane Austen in book sales.

points.h: Heavy pedagogy in her novels paradoxically caused her erasure
points.body: Edgeworth was most prolific from 1795 to 1815. She made a habit of embedding economic knowledge directly into her plots to educate readers. Jane Austen arrived slightly later with a more naturalistic narrative style, less overtly didactic. As readers' tastes shifted, Edgeworth's pedagogical approach became the very reason she disappeared from history. She herself called these works ‘moral tales’ rather than novels, since fiction was then viewed as frivolous entertainment for women.

points.h: She was the first generation to translate economics for ordinary readers
points.body: Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776, before Edgeworth began writing. Though her father never knew Smith personally, he knew all of Smith's friends, placing her at the front row of economics' birth. In an era of revolution and approaching industrialization, Edgeworth believed ordinary people needed to be taught this new intellectual framework—not, as later ideological fiction would do, simply commanded to adopt a given position.

points.h: Physics envy among economists gave birth to marginalism itself
points.body: Edgeworth's nephew, F.Y. Edgeworth, would later propose the famous Edgeworth box. In the mid-19th century, economists developed what became known as ‘physics envy’—a hunger to enter universities and be recognized as a rigorous science. They founded the all-male Political Economy Club. The marginalists rewrote utility theory as mathematical models. ‘Political economy’ itself was simplified into just ‘economics’ in Alfred Marshall's textbooks.

points.h: Her questions made Ricardo doubt his own comparative advantage theory
points.body: Edgeworth exchanged letters with David Ricardo for years, debating whether Ireland should devote itself entirely to potatoes. She restated Ricardo's own comparative advantage theory back to him, and he grew uneasy. He admitted that excessive specialization carried real risk—a concession he had never made publicly in his formal writings or in years of argument with Malthus. Shortly after, Ricardo died from an ear infection, and this moment of self-doubt never entered his published scholarly legacy.

points.h: Witnessing potato famine pushed her toward proto-Keynesian intervention
points.body: Edgeworth had previously been a strict believer in free trade, opposed to any poor-relief subsidies. Two potato famines—the first predating the famine history remembers—forced her to watch neighbors die in large numbers. This experience led her to revise her stance. She came to accept that extreme crises justified government intervention, even direct subsidies to the poor. This was a proto-Keynesian position, roughly eighty years ahead of Keynes himself. Before her death, one of her unfinished projects was a proposal that scholars study potatoes as Ireland's national food, with reference to her correspondence with Ricardo.

points.h: She backed the correct value theory before mainstream economics did
points.body: Smith, Ricardo, and Malthus—that generation of classical economists—all held the labor theory of value: that worth came from physical labor. In her novels, Edgeworth made a legally trained character, one doing no manual labor, the final victor, implying that value could derive from non-physical productive work. Her father went further in his letters, writing that Smith's theory contained errors and should be corrected through utility theory. The marginalists later proved this judgment was correct.

points.h: The AI era and 1800 face startlingly similar economic upheaval
points.body: Gina sees striking parallels between now and 1800: industrialization approaching but not yet arrived, agriculture suddenly more efficient, factories stoking fears of mechanized labor, and populist waves rippling through the aftermath of revolution. She is confident that AI will fundamentally change everything, though unsure when the real seismic shock arrives. Edgeworth wrote economic novels to help displaced workers understand their world and remain flexible as society turned upside down. This mirrors today's corporate emphasis on AI literacy—both eras needed people to stay adaptable through disruption.
